869.title: Love has boundaries
869.hook: love doesn't require letting yourself be harmed
869.howItsDone: Christians often point to the Gospel scenes where Jesus withdraws to pray as a pattern for rest and retreat, and people on many paths keep a sabbath, a quiet hour or a retreat as a protected time apart.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was love unreturned: love like Leah's, which still counts as love. Your line was still love.

People were coming and going, more of them than anyone could greet. In the Gospel of Mark, the disciples have just come back and told Jesus all they had done and taught, and the place is so busy, the text says, that they had no leisure so much as to eat. Nobody would blame a teacher for saying keep going, there's more to do. Instead Jesus says something else, and it's worth hearing on a day when the phone keeps buzzing and someone always needs one more thing.
screen: `COMING AND GOING.` → `NO LEISURE SO MUCH AS TO EAT.` → `JESUS SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the King James text Jesus tells them: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." Apart. Rest. In the middle of real need, with real people waiting. The Gospel doesn't treat this as a failure of love; it treats it as part of the work. Second, his own habit. Luke's Gospel says, in a short line, "he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." The same teacher who healed and fed and taught also walked away from the crowd, on purpose. Christians read this in more than one way, but the plain picture is a love with a shape: edges, and times of being unavailable. Third, the harder edge. When Jesus sends his followers out, Matthew's Gospel has him tell them that where a house or a city won't receive them, they should leave, and shake off the dust of their feet. Not fight. Not stay and be ground down. Leave, and keep the peace inside. Some readers find a principle in it: you can wish someone well and still walk out of their door. Fourth, what this means on an ordinary day. Love doesn't require letting yourself be harmed. A boundary isn't a wall to punish someone. It's a line that tells the truth about what you can carry. Saying no to one thing can be the way you keep saying yes to the people you love. And if anyone listening is in a situation where love is being used to hurt them, a boundary may mean getting help from someone you trust. That too can be love, including love for yourself.

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop and feel where your body ends, your skin, the chair under you, the floor under your feet; that edge isn't unkind, it's just where you are. Bring to mind one place in your life where a healthy boundary is needed, and without planning a speech, let one clear, simple sentence form, and hold it gently, without anger. If you pray, you can ask for courage in your own tradition's words.
Desert place. Where Jesus told his disciples to come apart and rest, even while the crowds still needed them. Today's word.
Your line: love has edges. Resting a while is part of the work, too. Until tomorrow.

870.title: Loving yourself rightly
870.hook: as yourself assumes you care for yourself too
870.howItsDone: In Buddhaghosa's instructions, loving-kindness practice begins by wishing oneself well before widening to others, and Jews study Hillel's sayings in Pirkei Avot, the Mishnah's collection of the sages' teachings.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was desert place, where Jesus said: come apart and rest a while. Your line was love has edges.

A king and a queen are talking privately, and the king asks her a question that sounds almost dangerous. Is there anyone, he says, dearer to you than yourself? A careful wife might be expected to say: you, my lord. She doesn't. She says no, there is no one dearer to her than herself, and then she asks him the same question. He gives the same answer. Then the king goes to the Buddha and tells him what they said. What the Buddha does with their honesty is the surprise.
screen: `ANYONE DEARER THAN YOURSELF?` → `NO, SAYS THE QUEEN.` → `THE KING ASKS THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: First, the story. It comes from the Pali scriptures, and the couple are King Pasenadi of Kosala and Queen Mallika. When the king brings their conversation to the Buddha, the Buddha doesn't scold either of them. He answers with a short verse. In plain words: search in every direction with your mind, and you will find no one dearer to anyone than their own self. Second, the turn. Because each person holds themselves dear in just this way, the verse says, one who loves oneself should not harm another. Self-love, here, isn't the opposite of kindness. It's the doorway. Each person knows from the inside how much they want to be safe and well, and that knowledge is the teacher. Third, the Torah makes a similar move. Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." As thyself. The command assumes a self being loved, a measure already in place. If the measure is broken, the neighbor gets a broken measure too. Fourth, the Jewish sage Hillel, who held both sides at once, is remembered in the Mishnah for three questions. In plain words: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? The first makes room for caring for yourself. The second keeps it from shrinking into selfishness. Rightly, then, means both: loving yourself enough to rest, to eat, to forgive your own mistakes, and remembering that everyone else is doing the very same, from the inside.

segments.voice: Place a hand on your chest or your stomach, feel its warmth, and notice whatever wish to be well is there, rested, safe, understood: a wish that isn't selfish, just human. Still with your hand there, let one other face come to mind, and remember that they want exactly the same thing, just as much, from the inside. If you pray, you can ask for both of you to be well, in words your tradition already has.

Your line: me too. Everyone you pass wants that too. Day eight hundred seventy, done.

871.title: Small acts
871.hook: love is mostly in small things
871.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of gathering merit little by little through everyday good deeds, Christians read the cup of cold water as a picture of small service, and the hadith in al-Tirmidhi counts a smile or removing harm from a path among acts of charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Queen Mallika, who said no one was dearer to her than herself. Your line was me too.

Drip. Drip. A leaky faucet over a bucket, or rain off the edge of a roof into a clay pot. Each drop is almost nothing. Nobody would bother to measure one. Leave the pot there overnight, though, and in the morning it's full to the brim. A verse in the Dhammapada, an old collection of the Buddha's sayings, uses exactly that picture, and not for water. For goodness. Three traditions speak to how small love can be and still count.
screen: `DRIP. DRIP.` → `EACH DROP IS ALMOST NOTHING.` → `IN THE MORNING, A FULL POT.`

segments.voice: First, the water-pot. In Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada, the verse warns against thinking lightly of good, as if it could never add up to much. Then comes the picture: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The wise, it says, become full of good the same way, gathering it little by little. No single drop fills the pot; every drop is part of the filling. Second, a cup of water. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says that whoever gives "a cup of cold water only" to one of his little ones, in the name of a disciple, "shall in no wise lose his reward." Notice the word only. Not a banquet. Not a fortune. Just water, and cold, which in a hot land is its own kindness. Third, a face. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in the collection of al-Tirmidhi, says in plain words that your smile in the face of your brother is charity. So, in the same saying, is guiding someone who is lost, or moving a stone out of the road. Charity, here, isn't only money. Fourth, what the three share, each in its own words. None of them says big acts don't matter. They say small ones aren't nothing. A text back. A door held. The dishes done without being asked. On an ordinary day, love often looks like that, and these teachers say it adds up.

segments.voice: Breathe slowly and let the day ahead come to mind, the places you'll be and the people you'll see, and find three small kindnesses that fit inside it: a glass of water poured for someone, a real smile at the counter, a message that says thinking of you. See each one clearly, one at a time, the way a drop falls. If you pray, you can offer the day in your own tradition's words.
Small acts. Kindnesses too small to measure one by one, the drop, the cup of water, the smile, that fill the pot over time. Today's word.
Your line: small things. Nobody needs to measure the drops for the pot to fill. That's day eight hundred seventy-one.

872.title: Listening as love
872.hook: listening may be love's most common form
872.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema, which opens with the word hear, in daily prayer; in Jewish mourning, by custom, visitors to a house of mourning wait for the mourner to speak first, and people on many paths practice listening as a form of care in chaplaincy and friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was small acts: drops that fill the pot over time. Your line was small things.

Halfway through a friend's story, a sentence starts forming. A better story. A piece of advice. The same thing happened to me. The friend is still talking, but the mind has already left the room to rehearse. It's a moment with two sides: the one waiting to speak, and the one who can tell they're not really being heard. Two old texts, from the letter of James and from the book of Job, point at another way to be in a conversation.
screen: `A SENTENCE STARTS FORMING.` → `THE MIND LEAVES THE ROOM.` → `ANOTHER WAY TO BE THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the order of things. The letter of James, in the King James Bible, puts it in a single line: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Swift to hear comes first. Not clever to answer. Not quick with advice. The ears come ahead of the mouth. Second, a picture of it done well. In the book of Job, everything has been taken from Job: his children, his health, his wealth. Three friends come to comfort him, and at first they do something remarkable. "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." They don't explain. They don't fix. They stay. Third, what happens next. Eventually the friends start talking, for chapters, explaining why this must have happened to him. Some readers notice that the friends were at their best in the silence, and went wrong when they started to speak. At the end of the book, the text says God is not pleased with what they said about him. Fourth, a word from Hebrew that holds all of this. A prayer said in Jewish worship, from the book of Deuteronomy, begins with Shema: hear, or listen. In that prayer, listening comes first. Listening isn't a pause before the real love begins. It can be the love. Full attention says, without a single word, you matter enough for me to stop.

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or let them rest low, and just listen: first the farthest sound you can hear, then something closer in the room, then the closest of all, your own breath, letting each arrive and leave without naming or judging it. When your mind starts composing something to say, notice it and come back to listening, the same muscle a friend needs from you. If you pray, you can listen in your own tradition's way.
Shema. The opening word of a Jewish prayer that means hear, or listen, placing attention before any answer. Today's word.
Your line: just listen. Sometimes the kindest answer is your full attention. See you tomorrow.

873.title: Love and grief
873.hook: grief is love with nowhere to go, as many say
873.howItsDone: Traditions mark grief in their own ways: Jewish mourners sit shiva, Christians hold funerals and remember the dead in prayer, Muslims pray the funeral prayer and visit the family, Hindus and Sikhs each hold their own rites and recitations for the departed, and many Buddhists chant and make offerings in their name.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Shema: hear, or listen. Your line was just listen.

A coat still hangs by the door, months later. Nobody wears it. Nobody can move it either. A phone holds a voicemail that never gets deleted. A recipe card sits in a drawer in handwriting that won't come again. Small things, and they can stop a person cold in the middle of an ordinary afternoon. People sometimes put it this way: grief is love with nowhere to go. In the Gospel of John, there's a scene where grief and love show up side by side, in the same breath.
screen: `A COAT STILL BY THE DOOR.` → `A VOICEMAIL NEVER DELETED.` → `GRIEF AND LOVE, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. Jesus has a friend named Lazarus, in the village of Bethany, with his sisters Martha and Mary. Lazarus falls sick and dies before Jesus arrives. When Jesus comes, Mary falls at his feet weeping, and the people with her are weeping too. Jesus asks where they have laid him. Then comes a verse of two words, in the King James text: "Jesus wept." Second, what the onlookers see. They don't say, look how sad he is. The text has them say, "Behold how he loved him!" Standing by a grave, they read his tears as love: the grief was the shape the love took. Third, the surprise. In John's story, Jesus is about to call Lazarus out of the tomb. The ending is close. And still he weeps. Some Christians see in it that hope doesn't cancel grief; the loss is real, and it's honored with tears. Fourth, the line from the hook. It's a saying, not a scripture, but it fits the scene. Love that used to have a phone number, a chair at the table, a person to reach now has nowhere to land, so it comes out as tears, or as a coat that can't be moved. Seen this way, grief isn't a sign that something went wrong with you. It's evidence of what was there. Different traditions hold death and what follows it in very different ways, and this lesson won't choose among them. But on any path, the tears can be read the way the people at Bethany read them.
screen: `A FRIEND NAMED LAZARUS.` · `BEHOLD HOW HE LOVED HIM.` · `HE WEEPS ANYWAY.` · `LOVE WITH NOWHERE TO GO.` · then, large: `JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: If it feels right today, bring to mind one grief, a person, a place, a pet, a time of life, a friendship that ended; if nothing comes, that's fine too, just sit with the breath. If something does come, let it be there without fixing it, and quietly say beside it, not instead of it: it was love. If tears come, let them; if you pray, you can hold this one in your own tradition's words.
Bethany. The village where Lazarus died, and where the onlookers watched Jesus weep and said, behold how he loved him. Today's word.
Your line: it was love. A loss that still catches you off guard is love, remembering. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

874.title: St Valentine
874.hook: an early Christian martyr whose day became about love, 14 February
874.howItsDone: Some churches still keep a feast of St Valentine on February 14, and around the world the day is marked by giving cards, notes and flowers to partners, friends and family.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Bethany, where Jesus wept and the people said, behold how he loved him. Your line was it was love.

Red paper hearts taped to a classroom window. A drugstore aisle that turns pink overnight. Roses by the bucket, and a wait for every table. In plenty of countries, February the fourteenth has become the day for saying I love you out loud. But the name on the day belongs to someone the cards never mention: a Christian remembered as a martyr, whose story is mostly lost. Today starts a short run of days of love, kept by different traditions.
screen: `RED PAPER HEARTS.` → `A NAME ON THE DAY.` → `A STORY MOSTLY LOST.`

segments.voice: First, the honest part. Tradition says Valentine was a Christian in the early centuries of the church, in or near Rome, who was put to death for his faith. Beyond that, the record is thin. Old church lists remember more than one martyr named Valentine, and it isn't clear whether the stories are about one man or several. When the sources are this quiet, it's worth saying so. Second, the stories people tell. One legend has him marrying couples in secret when marriage was forbidden to soldiers. Another has him healing his jailer's daughter and leaving her a note signed, from your Valentine. These are stories, told and retold, not facts anyone can check, and they're loved anyway. Third, how a martyr's day became a lovers' day. Long afterward, the English poet Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a poem, the Parliament of Fowls, set on Saint Valentine's day, when every bird comes to choose its mate. Some scholars think that poem, and others like it, helped tie the saint's day to romance. Nobody can say for certain how the change happened. Fourth, what's left when the legends are set aside: a person remembered by Christians as faithful unto death, and a day the world uses to say, plainly, I love you. Some churches still remember him on that day. And one modern custom fits the legend of the note: writing it down, telling someone on paper what they mean to you.
screen: `A MARTYR, THE RECORD THIN.` · `THE STORIES PEOPLE TELL.` · `CHAUCER'S BIRDS CHOOSE MATES.` · `WRITE IT DOWN.` · then, large: `ST VALENTINE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who would be glad to hear from you, a partner, a parent, a friend, a teacher, a child, not necessarily the obvious one, and let their face come clear. Then let one true, plain sentence form about what they mean to you, something like you made that year easier, and hold it until it feels right. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own tradition's words.
St Valentine. A Christian remembered as a martyr, little known for certain, whose day became a day for telling people you love them. Today's word.
Your line: a note. One plain sentence can carry a lot of love. Until tomorrow.

875.title: Tu B'Av
875.hook: the fifteenth of Av, once a day when young women danced in white in the vineyards (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)
875.howItsDone: Some Jews today mark Tu B'Av as a day of love, with weddings, matchmaking events and celebrations, and Jews who study the Mishnah read about it in tractate Taanit.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was St Valentine, a martyr whose day became a day for saying it on paper. Your line was a note.

Rows of vines outside Jerusalem. Young women walk out between them, all dressed in white, and begin to dance. It sounds like the opening of a romance, but it's in the Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law and teaching, at the close of a section about fast days. In the middle of all that seriousness, a rabbi stops to remember a day of pure joy. Its name is a date on the Hebrew calendar: the fifteenth of the month of Av.
screen: `ROWS OF VINES.` → `ALL DRESSED IN WHITE.` → `A RABBI REMEMBERS JOY.`

segments.voice: First, the saying. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says, in plain words, that Israel had no days of joy like the fifteenth of Av and the Day of Atonement. On those days, the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white garments and danced in the vineyards. Second, the detail that makes the passage. The white garments were borrowed, the Mishnah says, so as not to shame anyone who had none of her own. Rich or poor, nobody could tell. On a day about love, the first act was a kindness about dignity. Third, what they said. The young women called out to the young men, in plain words: lift up your eyes and see whom you choose; don't look at beauty, look at family. The Mishnah then reads a line from the Song of Songs about a king on the day of his wedding, and the gladness of his heart. Fourth, the name. Tu is the number fifteen written in Hebrew letters, and Av is the month, so the name is simply the date. The vineyard dances belong to the past. Some Jews mark the day today as a day for love, for weddings and for matchmaking, a happy turn in a month that also holds the mourning of Tisha B'Av. This week traced love's edges: boundaries, loving yourself, small acts, listening, grief, and a note. Tu B'Av adds one more: when love dances, nobody gets left out of the white.
screen: `NO DAYS OF JOY LIKE THESE.` · `THE WHITE BORROWED.` · `LIFT UP YOUR EYES.` · `THE NAME IS THE DATE.` · then, large: `TU B'AV.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time someone made sure you weren't left out, an invitation, a seat saved, a coat lent, a word that put you on equal footing, and stay with it for a breath or two. Then let one person around you who might be on the outside right now come to mind, someone new, someone quiet, someone without the right thing to wear in whatever sense, and simply hold them kindly. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
